UME Native Plants Redesign
CHRISTINE GOMES · UX CASE STUDY
Research Synthesis Iteration Final design Reflection
UX research & product design, spring 2025

Growing an easier way to find the right native plant.

A semester-long redesign of the University of Maryland Extension's native plant resource. We took a static, hard-to-search database and turned it into a personalized, accessible tool for home gardeners, landscapers, nurseries, and state agencies.

THE BRIEF

UME already runs one of the largest native-plant knowledge bases in the state: scientific classifications, growing conditions, benefits to pollinators, landscaping guidance, all of it. What it didn't have was a way to help four very different audiences actually use that knowledge. Search and filtering were limited, content had no personalization, and the database structure just didn't match how people actually looked for plants.

Our brief started out simple: "improve the UX." Through background research and client conversations, it grew into something more specific. Build a Plant Toolkit that lets people generate a custom garden plan from their own site conditions, and an intuitive search and filtering system tuned to each stakeholder group, all of it accessible to WCAG standards from the start.

Phase 01: Research & discovery

Understanding who was actually getting stuck, and where.

We split discovery into two tracks running in parallel: a competitive read of how other native-plant resources solve the same problem, and a direct survey of the people who'd actually use ours.

METHOD

We looked closely at six major native-plant resources: Audubon, National Wildlife Federation, USDA PLANTS, Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center, Virginia DCR, and Homegrown National Park. We compared them on modernity, usability, functionality, content scope, and unique features, mostly just trying to figure out what to borrow and what to steer clear of.

Audubon Native Plants Database

Strength
ZIP-based recommendations, modern filters.
Drawback
Bird-focused; narrow ecological scope.
Takeaway
Location-based finder, clean UI.

National Wildlife Federation

Strength
ZIP-based wildlife recommendations.
Drawback
Wildlife-only; thin plant detail.
Takeaway
Pair with expert-backed content.

USDA PLANTS Database

Strength
Comprehensive, rigorous taxonomy.
Drawback
Overwhelming for casual users.
Takeaway
Balance accuracy with approachability.

Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center

Strength
Modern, rich multimedia and video.
Drawback
Non-native plants blur the focus.
Takeaway
Multimedia, kept strictly on-topic.

Virginia DCR

Strength
Practical, region-specific guidance.
Drawback
Limited interactivity.
Takeaway
Add maps and care checklists.

Homegrown National Park

Strength
Community-driven restoration angle.
Drawback
Dense, cluttered presentation.
Takeaway
Keep community features visually calm.
SURVEY
9 respondents · 5 intermediate, 4 expert gardeners

Our 14-question survey covered general experience, navigation, content quality, and accessibility on UME's existing site. The answers were consistent enough to act on immediately:

"I don't know what the home page is. I generally just use the search bar."Q2 · first impression
"Not really. It is difficult to find specific information without using the search bar."Q7 · is the site intuitive?
"Filtering by conditions (sun, shade, soil) and a side-by-side plant comparison tool."Q4 · what would help most
"Maybe, but I would use it more if it had a plant comparison tool."Q14 · would you return?

Respondents converged on the same must-haves at a glance: common and scientific name, sun/soil/moisture needs, ecological benefits, and mature size, plus requests for dark mode, larger tap targets, and better print support.

Phase 02: Synthesis

Turning survey answers into three people we could design for.

We ran every response through affinity diagramming, grouped them into six themes, and built personas around the patterns that mattered most: a plant enthusiast, a curious home gardener, and a landscape professional.

WHY IT MATTERED

The affinity groups weren't just something we filed away. They became the five filter categories in the final search tool (region, plant type, sun exposure, soil texture, soil moisture) and the backbone of the Plant Toolkit's "build your own" flow. Every flow we mapped had to work for all three personas before we let ourselves sketch a single screen.

Phase 03: Ideation & iteration

From a whiteboard free-for-all to something testable.

We started with a "Crazy Four," everyone sketching four layout ideas in a fixed time box, then converged on paper wireframes, tested them on the whiteboard, and rebuilt them in Figma once the structure held up.

MID-FI
Built in Figma, tested with users

Once the whiteboard sketches held up under a walkthrough, we rebuilt the key screens as grayscale Figma wireframes: search tool, saved-plants profile, "popular at the moment," and the plant-matching tool. We used those in usability sessions before we let ourselves touch color or type.

Phase 04: The final design

A high-fidelity prototype UME can build against.

The finished prototype layers three things on top of UME's existing brand: dynamic, stakeholder-specific search and filtering; a Plant Toolkit for building a custom garden plan; and accessible defaults throughout, from contrast to tap targets.

01 / Search & filter

Five filters, tuned to the six themes from research.

Region, plant type, sun exposure, soil texture, and soil moisture sit up front; "show more filters" expands into the deeper criteria power users asked for, without burying the simple case.

02 / Search results

Removable filter tags, so refining never feels like starting over.

Applied filters surface as tags above the results grid: visible proof of what's shaping the list, and a one-click way to loosen a search that's come back too narrow. Three separate survey answers called out that exact frustration, so it felt worth solving well.

03 / Plant Matcher

A swipe-based matcher for people who don't know what they're looking for yet.

Built directly for personas like Suki, our curious home gardener persona, someone who finds long filter lists overwhelming. Include/exclude preferences narrow the deck, and each card carries tolerances, garden uses, and wildlife benefits at a glance.

04 / Plant Toolkit

Pre-built gardens for browsing, a goal-based generator for building.

"Browse Gardens" hands over curated rain, butterfly, sun, and shade palettes for people who just want a fast answer. "Build your own" turns a single goal, something like "I want to attract pollinators," into a suggested plant list, and links straight into the Matcher for anyone who wants to keep refining.

05 / My Plants

Saved without an account, because most people told us they'd skip one.

Survey respondents were pretty candid about not wanting to sign up for a resource they'd only use occasionally. So we designed "My Plants" to work off local, on-device storage by default: fast, private, no forms to fill out, while still leaving the door open to an optional account for cross-device access down the road.

Decision log

Accounts vs. no accounts: the debate we didn't skip past.

This is the kind of trade-off research surfaces and doesn't resolve on its own. We laid out both sides before deciding.

The case for an account

Personalized collections ("Shade Garden," "Pollinator-Friendly"), access from any device, seasonal reminders, and secure, durable storage that survives a cleared browser.

What we shipped instead

A "Save Plant" button backed by local storage. Zero sign-up friction, nothing collected, works right away. The trade-off: saves are device-specific and disappear if browser data gets cleared, which we flagged as a good candidate for an optional account layer down the line.
What got in the way

Six things that pushed back on the plan.

Broad scope, thin plant knowledge

None of us started out as native-plant experts. We scoped foundational research early and stayed focused on user experience over plant taxonomy, since that was never really ours to solve.

A parallel database project

Another student team was rebuilding UME's underlying plant database at the same time. We drew a hard line: our deliverable was experience and interface, not back-end data management, and said so clearly in every handoff.

Mobile expectations vs. timeline

The client wanted a mobile version. Building both desktop and mobile prototypes in one semester just wasn't realistic, so we told them early and delivered mobile-friendly recommendations for the next phase instead of rushing a second prototype.

Users didn't want accounts

It came up again and again in survey answers, completely unprompted. Rather than override what people were telling us, we designed around it (see the decision log above).

Six schedules, one meeting time

When2Meet, Doodle, and a shared calendar got us into the same room; async responsiveness between meetings was the harder muscle to build.

Keeping workload even across a large team

Shared task ownership and regular check-ins kept six people moving at the same pace without anyone quietly picking up the slack.

Handoff

What we'd tell the next team to do first.

The prototype is a foundation, not a finished product. Our recommendations to UME were specific about what comes next.

Formal usability testing

Structured sessions with real home gardeners, landscapers, nurseries, and state agency staff to pressure-test the interface we designed around survey data alone.

Mobile-responsive design

A full mobile build for on-the-go use: in a garden center, in a yard, phone in hand.

Live plant data

Connect the front end to UME's actual native-plant database so search and filtering run on real records, not prototype content.

Optional accounts

Layer in accounts for cross-device saved lists and reminders, without making them mandatory.

Assistive-tech testing

Manual screen-reader and keyboard testing against WCAG 2.1, plus automated audits with WAVE or Axe.

Stakeholder-specific views

Explore dedicated "Consumer," "Designer," and "Agency" pathways so each audience sees what's relevant to them first.

"This project has enhanced UME's ability to share its valuable native plant knowledge in a more user-friendly and impactful way."
